utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. For the record, all the accused are here. Defence teams, full house except for Mr. Haynes. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey. I understand you have a preliminary, Mr. McCloskey. Before you do so, just for the record, we are starting with a half-hour delay because there was a technical hitch, which was beyond our control, and we had to wait until it was fixed. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Could we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. For the record, while we were in private session, we were discussing the putting into place possible protective measures that have been asked by the witness. We've heard both parties, and we have decided to put an application of facial distortion only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Simanic, and welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence. There are a few things I would explain to you; but, before you testify, you are required to make a solemn declaration under our Rules that you will be testifying the truth. That's the equivalent of an oath in some jurisdictions. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. There are two reasons why you were kept waiting before coming into the courtroom. One is we had a technical problem. We have fixed that. The second is that Mr. McCloskey, for the Prosecution, has informed us that during his proofing sessions with you, you expressed the desire to have in place some protective measures. We have discussed that. We have also heard the members of the Defence teams, and everyone is in agreement that the only protective measure that we can grant you is to hide your face from the public. We call that facial distortion. Basically, that means that no one will be able to see your face from outside the four walls of this courtroom. I hope that puts you more at ease, satisfies you. I'd like to know whether you're happy with this arrangement so that we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only partially happy; but if that's all I can get, then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I can assure you that we would have granted you more protective measures if we were satisfied that there was a good cause shown for them, but there isn't, not according to our Rules. You will now be asked some questions by Mr. McCloskey, and he will then be followed by the various members of the Defence teams on cross-examination. However, before we start with the questions, it is my duty to alert you to a provision that we have in our Rules which protects your right against self-incrimination. Let me explain, in simple words, what I mean. Our Rules provide that if a question is put to you which, if answered truthfully by you, could expose you to any possible criminal proceedings in the future, then you can address us, the four Judges here, and ask us to exempt you from answering such questions. I'm not saying that there will be such questions, but I cannot exclude them, either, because I don't know what questions will be asked. If any such questions are put to you and you ask for an exemption from us answering that question or those questions, then we have two options. We can either accept your plea and grant you an exemption, or we can decide not to exempt you but rather to compel you to give a truthful answer to such questions. In such a case, if we compel you to answer such a question, there is a further right that you enjoy; namely, that unless your testimony amounts to false testimony, then whatever you say in answering such questions cannot be used against you in any possible future proceedings that could be taken against you. Have I made myself clear to you? Have you understood the import of my explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe so. I'm not a lawyer, you know, so I have been able to understand as much as I can, in my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you at least understand that you have a right to ask us not to answer incriminatory questions, questions that, if answered truthfully, could expose you to criminal proceedings? Have you understood that, at least?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then I think we can safely proceed. Mr. McCloskey, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simanic. Can you, first of all, tell us your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: My name is Mile Simanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what year were you born?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I was born in 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I grew up in Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina, the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I am a construction engineer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly outline your education leading to your profession as a construction engineer?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Having completed the elementary school in Sekovici, I also completed a secondary construction school in Tuzla, and I went to university in Sarajevo, where I also graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what degree did you graduate in from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I obtained a degree in Engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what year was that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: That was in 1981.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do your JNA service at some point?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when was that and where?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: In 1977 and 1978, in Tuzla and in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, before the war broke out in 1991 and 1992, did you have a chance to work in your profession as a construction engineer?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just briefly tell us what work you were involved in before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: On the eve of the war, I worked in the Self-Governing Interest Community of Vlasenica. The abbreviation is "SIZ."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you involved in engineering projects, construction projects?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, my institution had its officials which were in charge of supervising certain works and designing certain projects, and I was in charge of all of that, and, finally, I was involved with the Assembly of Self-Governing Interest Communities, which is very much like the Association of Assemblies. People were appointed to these institutions, and there were also clients who chose these institutions to perform certain construction works for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, can you give us an idea of the kind of work projects and construction we're talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I worked on the construction of local roads within the municipality, constructing various infrastructure in the municipality. To a certain extent, I was also involved in residential construction; and in some instances, when we had to change certain aspects of those designs, we would also act as planners or designers. I was not the only person involved in these projects. We worked in teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you again now briefly outline your military assignments, what units you were in when the war broke out? If you can start from, let's say, the summer of 1992 and go onward.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was mobilised, I was assigned to the Territorial Defence of the Municipality of Vlasenica. We were headquartered at the Panorama Hotel. We were assigned to some companies, and all these companies differed. In addition to that, the Army of Republika Srpska was established, and the Territorial Defence remained in place until the end of that year. After that, the Drina Corps was established, and then it was divided up into units according to the corps requirements. We were assigned to companies and battalions on the strength of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's just jump to 1995. Can you tell us what position you held in the beginning of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy of the Engineering Battalion of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what the name of that Engineering Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It was the 5th Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was your title "Deputy Commander" of that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was your commander in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: My commander in 1995 was Milenko Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe, just broadly during the year of 1995, what sort of work were you involved in for the 5th Engineers?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Commander Avramovic and I divided all the jobs between ourselves. I was in charge of the construction works for the army because that was my field of expertise. I was well versed in all sorts of road construction works. Commander Avramovic, on the other hand, was involved with other tasks which were mostly of a military nature. I did not interfere with those because I did not find myself versed in those matters, so I didn't get involved in such duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we can understand what road building involves. What military-type engineering projects are you referring to that Avramovic would have concentrated on?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I'm mostly talking about minefields, laying mines and clearing minefields; and the rest, I don't understand much about all that. That's why I can't use the military terminology. I also didn't know much about military administration that both him and higher units insisted on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In 1995, did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I started as captain first class, and then I was promoted to the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was Commander Avramovic's rank?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: He also started as captain first class, and he was also promoted to the rank of major later on, but I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say you were the deputy commander. What was your position when Mr. Avramovic left the area of the Drina Corps or was absent?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, I should have stood in for him, but our unit, our battalion, was almost always deployed in various construction sites, where they performed various construction tasks. Somebody had to be in charge of all of that. So when he was absent, I primarily made sure that all the construction sites were working properly. As for the command part of his job, I did not find that very important in Konjevic Polje. I spent most of the time at various construction sites, where I made sure that the works followed the schedule that were -- schedules that were required from us from our superior units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But did you take over command when he was absent?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Conditionally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you mean, "conditionally speaking"? I don't think command is a conditional situation, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, what I'm saying is that when it comes to the military administration, I didn't understand much about that, so that whenever somebody told me how things should be done, how things should be written, I just did that. I did not question things too much. On the other hand, when I was in a construction site, I understood the matter much better. I could issue orders, I could supervise things, and I could stand by everything I did on a construction site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to July 1995, and can you tell us, for that time period, a little bit about the structure of the 5th Engineers? First of all, can you tell us about the personnel? How many people were in this battalion, and how were they divided up in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know the exact number, so in a conversation with my lawyer, I got the exact number. I believe that there were a total of 134 men in the battalion, out of whom 111 are foot soldiers and the remainder were the so-called command staff. We were deployed on various construction sites in Han Pogled above Vlasenica. This is where we worked. We were involved in the construction of the so-called passive light for the telephone network of Vlasenica. At the time, Vlasenica was not connected to any of the other towns, so we had to complete that part of the job in order to connect Vlasenica and put it into the telephone network of Republika Srpska. Our next job that I wasn't involved in, however, was works on Vis, near Mount Kalesija. A larger group of engineers from the Engineering Battalion worked there. We also had a construction site in the Bisina Barracks near Sekovici. We were involved in the barracks construction there. We also worked in Crna Rijeka, near Han Pijesak, where the command was, the army command. As far as I know, some prefabricated buildings were being erected there to accommodate the army. In Vlasenica, we also had a workshop, where we had people involved in the repairs and maintenance of various buildings. We had our plumbers and electricians there, who would be called to repair the appointments in houses that had been damaged or to maintain the army buildings. One part of our unit was in Konjevic Polje, in the rear, where that part of the unit was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What sort of building was the unit in, in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje, we were billeted in several private houses that were damaged. We repaired them and then we used them either to billet the troops or to store the goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you use a school near the intersection of Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: We used just one part of the school. We used a classroom that we converted into an office. We transformed the boiler house into our kitchen, and we used this classroom, not as an office but as a dining room. We changed the door so that the door led from the kitchen to the dining room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that you had many construction projects in the area, but can you tell us where Avramovic's command office was? Where did he command from, generally, when he wasn't in the field at the various construction sites?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I was the one who was mostly spending time at construction sites. As for Mr. Avramovic, he was in Konjevic Polje, where we had an office in a building there. And when he wasn't in Konjevic Polje, as far as I was told, I was told wherever the commander is, that's where the command post is. The 5th Engineering Battalion did not have its area of responsibility. It was only deployed there for the purpose of storing its things. Our first command was in Vlasenica; then we were moved to Milici, near the playground. There was not enough space there. There was not enough storage space, and that's why we were further moved to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you in Konjevic Polje in July 1995, the offices and the buildings you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your unit.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: One part of the unit was in Konjevic Polje, indeed. The troops who would return from leave, especially those who hailed from Zvornik and the area around it, they would first report to Konjevic Polje and then they would be dispatched to various construction sites. Konjevic Polje was the place where the rear platoon was mostly billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were not at various construction sites, did you have an office place where you did your business in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: When I was not at a construction site or when I was preparing for some construction works, I stayed at Konjevic Polje to complete that part of the job; and, from there, I would go and work at construction sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Besides the Konjevic Polje facility and the repair shop you've described in Vlasenica, did the 5th Engineers have any other office space or facility somewhere else? And I'm talking about July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: We did not have any other offices, as the one in Milici was closed down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any -- or describe what sort of construction equipment the Engineering Battalion had in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You mean all of our equipment and where it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't need a complete inventory, but just the -- let's start with the excavating machines, excavators, loaders, that sort of thing, if you had any of those, and just tell us what you had and where they were.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It would be easier for me to just give you a breakdown of machinery per construction sites; for example, we had a loader machine. It was an older model, but it was still in good working order. It was in Pribicevac, which is above Sase. We were building a road three kilometres long, and this machine was commandeered by the Pribicevac Tactical Group, and it was engaged on repairing that road. There were also two smaller lorries, the so-called 13 lorries, that worked alongside that loader. Also, we had a small bulldozer, TG110, which was on Vis, working on the construction of an ancillary road and protective barriers along that road. There was also a tractor there. It had a small digging bucket in the back, and in front it had a small loading bucket. It was there, and it was also at the Bisina Barracks. Furthermore, we had four or five big boats with strong engines which were not in a good state of repair. They called them barges, and we also had three scaffolding sets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think, as we hear the translation, when you're talking about boats and scaffolding sets, are you talking about a military pontoon bridge that would form a bridge across a river? I'm getting a signal that he may not have got the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I heard some comment coming from some of the accused. Do you have the same problem. You did not receive -- did you receive interpretation of Mr. McCloskey's question? They seem to have received it. Perhaps you could repeat your question, kindly, Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the accused have not received the interpretation, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am sorry about that. I thought --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that now it's working, the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Could you kindly repeat your question, Mr. McCloskey, please. And thank you, Madame Fauveau, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you described boats and a scaffolding, were they associated with your pontoon company and, pardon my B/C/S, but "pontonjerska ceta"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the Pontoon Company equipment. But, again, when you say "company," you have to take this term conditionally. When you say "a company," you imply about 100 men, but we only had about 16 or 17 people who were working in that company and who were in charge of guarding those tugboats or bridges, pontoon bridges places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did your company operate a pontoon bridge across the Drina in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: We did not have a pontoon bridge, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have a ferry crossing that the Pontoon Company looked after somewhat?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: We just called it a crossing. There was some elements and boats and iron rope across the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that located, that we'd call it a ferry?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: There were three places: Osamsko, Fakovici, and -- three places. I believe that Petrica was the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did supplies come over from Serbia from those ferries in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: As far as I knew and as far as I was informed, there was no supply through us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a supply through someone else?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Possibly. I was not aware of it, and I was not informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We may ask about that a bit later. Aside from the excavating machines you've mentioned, did your battalion have the ability, either itself or through the corps, to requisition other excavation or construction equipment for various projects?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, the battalion never required other machines and never applied for other machines, because if they would order us to carry out certain works, then we would go to do some reconnaissance, see what kind of works and what their scope was, and what the battalion was able to do. If the battalion was unable to cope with something, then the corps had to issue an order specifying in which way it would be done, whether the machines of the 5th Engineering would be resubordinated to some other unit or the task would be accomplished in some other way, whether they would give our machines to whichever unit was going to actually perform the works. That was how it was usually done. We would make our machines available, and the corps would provide other machines and logistics. By "logistics," I mean fuel, lubricants, and everything that is necessary to carry out that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And besides yourself, who was an actual engineer, can you tell us what Avramovic's professional position was in terms of his professional qualifications as an engineer?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: He was not an engineer. He had graduated from the military academy, and I believe his branch was engineering, which is different from a construction engineer, working in civil engineering with appropriate degrees and diplomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from yourself, as a construction engineer, were there any other qualified construction engineers on the 5th Engineering Battalion in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go into some more particular dates in July, and I now want to take you to that time period that you may remember when the Srebrenica enclave fell or was liberated, depending on your position. Do you remember that period of time when Srebrenica -- when General Mladic marched through Srebrenica and Srebrenica became Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact dates, but we watched it on television later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We don't need to really worry about exact dates. I'll mention some dates that will help us get oriented, but it's more the time period that I'm concerned about, and I think we can go from there. But just for your knowledge, and everyone will agree, that Mladic and others went through Srebrenica for the first time on 11 July 1995. So can you tell me where you were at that time? Where were you watching television or where were you when Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: If that was on the 11th, then my movements were approximately from Konjevic Polje to Vlasenica, and I went to those places touring construction sites that mostly concentrated around Vlasenica, and that is why I spent most of my time in Vlasenica, because at that time I was also involved in some other preparations for other construction sites that were about to be opened, and they were related to Vlasenica. We were supposed to build the road for the requirements of the Vlasenica Brigade towards Kladanj to enable supply to units, and we also had to prepare the ground for the building of transmission lines from Vlasenica to Konjevic Polje, because Vlasenica at the time had no electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know where your commander was on this day that Srebrenica fell, 11 July?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, during those days, he was absent. His wife and daughter had come to visit from Slovenia. I don't remember when he left, but we didn't see each other immediately before he left. I was just told, notified, that he would not be there for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so who was in command of the 5th Engineering Battalion in the absence of Major Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I just said a moment ago, conditionally speaking, it was me; but when I was not in Konjevic Polje, there was a duty officer who was perfectly able to deal with everything, just as the commander would have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a daily report requirement for the 5th Engineers to report their activities to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a bit about that, what you were -- what the requirements were? And we'll go over, as you know, one of those reports a little bit later, but if you could tell us generally.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, the administrator, who was in Konjevic Polje, and the duty officer knew where the units were deployed. That would be put in the report, and I would sign that report in the absence of Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to the time Srebrenica has fallen. Mladic has gone through. You're in the area of Konjevic Polje, and you say you're going to Vlasenica. Were you aware of any activity, any Muslim movement, from the direction of the former enclave through the area of Konjevic Polje, Milici, Gravica?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, officially speaking, we did not receive a single notification of that in Konjevic Polje; but most of the information that we were unable to verify even, we received from soldiers who were returning from home leave. This was unverified information, but that was all we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But what information did you have?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, it's written in one of the reports that a large group of enemy soldiers had been inserted and that they were in the broader area of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you see any of these Muslim soldiers or civilians passing through the area when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where were you during this time period when there were reports that Muslims were going through this area?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly now whether I was in Konjevic Polje or in Vlasenica, but nobody passed through the barracks or through the immediate vicinity, so that we, or at least I, would be able to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What orders, if any, did you receive to defend your unit and your area from Muslims passing through the area?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: We did not receive any order to defend. It was our obligation, our standing obligation, to defend our barracks, because there were mines and explosives stored there. There was equipment and tools and personnel that had to be protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who commanded the defence of your barracks during this time period? And I'm talking about the 11th, the 12th, the 13th; the three days after Srebrenica fell.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, if I was not around, then there was the duty officer at the barracks who was responsible for the security of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, where were you during those three big days right after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I could only have been in Vlasenica or in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Which one, or what combination of? Those are fairly memorable days.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a long time ago. That's why I can't -- I was touring a number of construction sites; and depending on where I was needed, I would go to one of them. I can't tell you where I was on the 11th, on the 12th, on the 13th. I can't remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's, I believe, time for a break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you, just back to those combat reports, what time of day were you supposed to get the combat reports out to the Drina Corps by, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact time. Nobody asked us to submit them precisely at a certain hour. They had to be submitted within that day. Sometimes we were late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, can you get any more specific? Did they have to go out in the morning, or was it the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, I really couldn't say now when they were submitted, because we would put them in an envelope and give them to somebody who was going to Vlasenica, to take them, or use anybody who was going there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You didn't have one of those coded teletype machines?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, no way. We had an old machine, a typewriter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, there's one document that I want to go over with you. Perhaps it will refresh your recollection on some things. Its number is P02672. It's from the Command of the 5th Engineering Battalion, dated 14 July, and it says "By courier" on it, and it will come up on the screen there for you. I want to also give you the original that's got an original stamp and inked signature. Let's, first of all, turn it over on the back page or the second page, where we can see that it's typed up, and it says "Deputy Commander Major Mile Simanic." Do you see that signature on the original?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you remember what you told me last time we talked about this document, about who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what I said then, but sometimes I would sign a blank paper if I was not going to be there, so that the report could leave on time, be sent to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that what you think you did with this document, you just signed a blank?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but that kind of thing happened, because we didn't want any trouble from the Command. Therefore, I would sign a blank paper and then they would type the report on it, because these reports were stereotyped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting you would have signed your name to something, sent it to the Drina Corps, and not known the information that was on it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, as for the contents of the document, I was told that the important thing was the whereabouts of the unit, where it was deployed, and I mean the 5th Engineering Battalion. As for the rest, it was done according to a stereotype, and the person typing up the report would fill in the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can we put the original on the ELMO, because there's some inked material that may come up for Your Honours that you can see. I don't know if ELMO will catch it or not, but if we could try. Can you just pull it out of that plastic thing, Madam Usher, and it's a one-page document with material on the front and back. And if we could look first at the front, and if we could zero in a bit on the "1983" that appears to be handwritten on the top. Okay. That's good enough. I think ELMO's become colour-blind in the years we've had him, because we can't really see the colour there. Thank you. That's not -- we don't need the ELMO anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's now go over some of the information in this document. Why don't you -- you can hold that document in front of you, sir, so that it's easier to read. Let's start with the beginning. It's entitled "Regular Combat Report," and the first paragraph says -- now, you've had a chance to see this document during your interview which happened back in January of 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've had a chance to see this document yesterday and review it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So having reviewed the paragraphs of this document, can you tell us today whether or not you are responsible for the information in this document? In other words, did you sign off this document knowing the information in it when it was sent to the corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, as for this information about the enemy, I was not aware of that, and I didn't even look when I was signing because the unit that we belonged to had no way of checking the veracity of any information. This was probably entered based on what was learned from soldiers coming back from home leave. They must have told the administrator, and the administrator just put it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you believe that this information was on the document when you signed it, or do you believe that you signed a blank document and never saw this information?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I just told you I didn't read it. I don't know whether it was there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go over that first paragraph. It says, in English: "A large enemy group was infiltrated in the region of Pobudje Brdo and the region of Konjevic Polje. Units of the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP successfully resisted the enemy." Now, were you present on the 13th or 14th when the 5th Engineering Battalion and the MUP resisted the enemy, as stated in this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: On the 13th, as far as I can remember, I was not present, because this extraordinary event, this incident happened then, when two soldiers were wounded on the guard post. And this reference has to do with the fact that we were protecting the barracks, and our assignments were only around the guard posts around the barracks. I told you already I don't know how come MUP is in the same report, but this is done according to form, as I explained, and that's how this unit appears here. MUP has their check-points [as interpreted] on which they worked, following their own orders, and we had nothing to do with their work and no information about them. But since we had no losses, that's probably why the report says that the resistance was successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I'm Sorry. I don't want to disturb my colleagues --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's in order. The thing is that I would just like to clarify something that I heard, and here in the transcript I see a very slight difference. If I remember correctly, the witness said that MUP had their own check-point. It was in singular, and here it says "check-points."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Is that correct, Mr. Simanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had a check-point, one check-point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we would prefer that you not speculate about things. Can you tell us: Were you present on the 13th of July, the day before this report went out, in this area doing -- defending the area and your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I just told you a moment ago that I was not there when those people were wounded in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when were those people wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, according to this report, it was on the 13th of July, 1995, around 800 hours. That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's continue to the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, instead of you reading out, how about ask the witness to read it out and being translated by the interpreters, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you read slowly in your -- the sentence that begins: "About 1.000"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: This first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: "Around 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, in your view, does that sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no comma in the original B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember when I showed you this document in Bosnia, do you remember what you first said when you read that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I said, "God forbid," or "God Almighty," or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you say that after reading this sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Because at first I thought it was written meaning that the MUP and the Engineering unit did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you think what's described here was a crime, no matter who did it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I've already told you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think it might be an inappropriate question for the witness, and I do object because I think it calls for a legal conclusion. And unless we're given the same latitude with others, I think he should not answer that type of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think the witness is being asked to make a legal analysis as to whether all the ingredients of a possible crime are met here, you know, so I think it's a generic question. Yes, go ahead, Mr. McCloskey. And Mr. Simanic, if you could answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had started answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was: "Do you think, sir, what's described here in this document was a crime, no matter who did it?"

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Now I don't understand whether I'm supposed to answer or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're supposed to answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I have to answer, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: In my view, whoever does something like that, it constitutes a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue to go down the document, and I think I can read the rest for simplicity's sake. Thank you. Then, the second paragraph is entitled "Paragraph 2, BG," which we believe stands for "Combat Readiness." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it says: "The battalion was engaged on carrying out the following tasks:. And this is the -- the first one is, "(A), the 1st Pioneers Company," and I won't read all of it, but it talks about fighting the enemy in the region of Pobudje. It also talks about building fortifications in the area of Vis, and the clearing of mines in the region of Derventa. Can you tell the Court where Vis is? Vis is someplace fairly far away and doesn't have anything to do with Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The Vis facility is close to Kalesija, which is rather far from the place that you have in mind, that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the clearing of the mines in Derventa, where is Derventa?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Derventa is - just let me count it, how many kilometres from Konjevic Polje - 17 or 18 kilometres away from Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In what direction?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: In the direction of Milici; and from Milici, the road forks off to the mine, to the bauxite mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then we have the last sentence: "The squad sent to clear mines in Zeleni Jadar and Skelani region came back." We're all very familiar now with that region, so were you aware that some of your Pioneers were down there clearing mines before this date?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go to the next section, B. It talks about a road and bridge company, and it talks about some work at the Vlasenica PTT, which I think you've described. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it also says that this part of this road and bridge company was organising ambushes and engaged in combat activities against the enemy. So in these first two sections, A and B, we've got part of the Pioneers fighting the enemy, and now we have road and bridge guys organising ambushes. Were you aware that your Engineering Battalion guys were involved in this military defence activity?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I have just told you that those were defence activities which were being carried out in the barracks area. There were guards, and that's how the guards were organised in order to secure the barracks. All the available men were deployed at various guards' posts; and if a guard's post was critical, more men would be deployed there. And by the same token, if a guard's post was less critical, it required fewer men. Also, it had to be done in that way that they had to stay alert throughout the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then, again, let me call your attention to paragraph (a). It says: "Fighting the enemy" -- it says: "The Pioneers are fighting the enemy in the region of Pobudje." This Court has heard quite a bit of evidence about Pobudje. It's way out in the woods, up above the road between Konjevic Polje and Glavica, so that's not sitting -- that's not the barracks. Did you know anything about your unit being in the woods in Pobuje?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Look, Pobudje and Konjevic Polje are two places with a very indistinct border between them. When you say "Konjevic Polje," you don't know what it's meant, whether you mean Pobudje, the slopes of Pobudje, or what. In our view, Pobudje and Konjevic Polje were one and the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to C. It says: "The Engineering Company," and that's, I believe, the work you described at Crna Rijeka and the barracks there.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to D. We've spoken briefly about this, I think. It says: "The Pontoon Company organising ferry crossing points on the Drina River at the Osamsko, Fakovici, Petrica, and Sopotnik villages." Now, by "organising ferry crossing points," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The word speaks for itself, providing security for the ferry crossing points, which meant organising guard duty, providing security around the ferry crossing point in order to prevent looting and any such thing. That's the meaning of the word "security."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, were those ferries being used in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were not being used in June [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We got a translation that you said "June 1995." My question was: Were they being used in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I understood your question. You asked me about July, and I said that as far as I know, they were not being used at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So men are out there organising the ferry crossing points for ferries that are not being used?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I have to explain. Those were men from the neighbouring villages whom we engaged to be there and to provide security, and if need be to work on the ferries. As far as I know, in July, they did not do anything but provide security for the ferries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. We go down to E, and it says: "The Logistics Platoon," and it's providing logistic support to units organising combat activities against the enemy. So, again, we have part of the job of your logistics platoons is organising combat activities against the enemy. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, this may be a mistake. The word "organise" may be a mistake. There was very little available staff in Konjevic Polje. There were only one or two men from each company, and the Logistics Platoon is the only platoon that was down there, say, for the people who were on leave. In other words, they did not organise anything. They implemented or carried out things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know that from your memory? Does this help you refresh where you were and whether you were involved with them in that implementing, as you should have been as the man in command, or are you just speculating?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Look, the Logistics Platoon, as far as I know, could not organise anything. They could only implement or carry out tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. Were you commanding them in their implementation? Does this refresh your recollection that you were there, that you read this, that you reported this to your command, the Drina Corps, or is this -- are you just guessing?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I'm only saying how things should have been. MS. NIKOLIC [Interpretation] Your Honours, this question has been asked and answered on several occasions, and it has been answered very clearly by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, more or less, we are in agreement here, that it's true that the witness has already said now, "No, I told you I wasn't there." What is Mr. McCloskey doing here? Is he trying to refresh his recollection by these additional -- by referring him to these additional facts? So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if he still maintains the same position, then you proceed to your next question. Do you wish to repeat the question, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't think that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is your answer to that last question, whether this helps you remember whether you were there or not, is it the same? You can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I can't recall any new details. I'm just providing my comment to what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you stand by your testimony, that you don't recall being there and being involved in this, what is being identified in each of these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. That is an unnecessary question, because he's definitely answered it now. So you don't need to ask it again. His answer was he doesn't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to F, which is the -- it says: "MUP police company, executing tasks as ordered by its command, organising combat activities against the enemy in coordination with the units of the 5th Engineering Battalion." Now, in this paragraph, we see the 5th Engineering working with the MUP. Do you have any information that, at this time period, the 5th Engineering unit was working with and organising combat activities with the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: As I've already told you, there was a police check-point there in very close to the vicinity of our guards, post number 6, and the first right-hand side neighbour to this guards' post was the police check-point. That is why, I suppose, the word "coordination" is written in here. I have to say that the police and the army would very rarely or almost never cooperate or engage in any coordinated action, because there was a lot of antagonism between the police and the army. The police was much better equipped, which caused the feeling of jealousy among the troops who were not that well equipped as the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go down to -- there's a section about security and morale. It mentions that security measures were increased in the wider area of Konjevic Polje due to the infiltrated enemy, civilians, and soldiers. The morale of the soldiers arresting and fighting the enemy is high. Did you at the time have this information before you, wherever you were?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It doesn't say here who are arresting, but it says who are engaged in making arrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. It seems like a difference without a difference. Does that have a meaning to you, the difference you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No. What I am saying is that the 5th Engineering Battalion, as far as I know and as far as I can remember, never arrested anybody. They even had two wounded among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. It says the morale of the soldiers was high. Did you receive any information about how the soldiers morale was during those days?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I did not receive any such information. However, as soon as you have so few men in the barracks, their morale has to be high, because fear is always running much higher than anybody can assume. I suppose that this was written simply because nobody ran away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I will continue. The next one is number 4, entitled "Situation in the Territory." Again, it says: "A large enemy group infiltrated from the direction of Srebrenica into the region of Pobudje-Konjevic Polje." Then number 5 says: "Extraordinary Events." That talks about the wounding of these two soldiers from your unit that occurred on 13 July. Then number 6: "Logistics."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would like to see the original on the ELMO in B/C/S. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Usher. Okay. That has been attended to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Under the "Logistics" section, it says: "Preparatory activities need to be carried out for the loading machine which will be engaged to bury the killed enemy soldiers. Fifty litres of oil to be assigned for the task." Do you have any knowledge or information about the 5th Engineering unit using a loader to bury killed enemy soldiers, as referenced in this report?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you this: In my previous testimony, I said that this loader had remained in Pribicevac, and it continued together with the Tactical Group - I don't know in which direction - which means at that time it was not in Konjevic Polje, if you are talking only about the loader. We had another tractor, though. This was a small machine with a loading bucket in the back; and in front -- it was supposed to arrive from the Bisina Barracks where it had been engaged in some work. It was supposed to return, and I suppose this is the machine that was meant. And this part is what the Logistics is involved in, and they sent their requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why is it that you suppose that that is the machine being referenced here?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Which one do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The one you just mentioned. Why do you suppose that this little machine you've described is the one that's being referenced in paragraph 6?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I did not specify which machine. But since this was written by a person who did not know anything about the machines, I am explaining the difference between a loader, which is only used for loading, and that machine remained in Pribicevac as part of the Tactical Group in Pribicevac. The other machine, the machine that I'm referring to, we asked for this machine to be returned to us because of the works that we were supposed to do on the reconstruction of the electricity lines between Lastanica and Konjevic Polje. That's why I said that possibly it is this machine that is referred to herein.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you provide this Trial Chamber with any information about your unit engaged in burying the dead enemy [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of our unit being engaged in these activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the interpretation into the B/C/S of the question put by my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey, in line 9 in the B/C/S interpretation. I heard "fallen enemy soldiers"; whereas, in the transcript, we only have "dead enemy." And I suppose that the witness received the same interpretation I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think there's -- it doesn't change the meaning, really, of my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we thank Ms. Nikolic for pointing this out, but I don't think it, unless for the witness, makes a big difference or a material difference. He can proceed to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sometimes we have translation issues. Perhaps just to clarify it, I'll ask the question again, or I'll try to. Do you have any information of your unit involved in burying, you know, the killed soldiers that were referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I don't have any information about the involvement of this unit in burying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. At the time, the 13th, 14th, 15th, those days shortly after the fall of Srebrenica, were you aware that mass graves were dug in the area of Nova Kasaba, Cerska Valley, and Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go through the rest of this. We're almost done. Under "7", it says "Losses." There were none. Number 8, "Conclusions, Forecasts, Decisions." It talks about continuing organising ambushes to fight the enemy infiltrated in Pobudje Hill. "Shift the focus of the fight against them there. Destroy the enemy and liberate Pobudje Hill as soon as possible." So now we're talking about a specific area in Pobudje, the Pobudje Hill, and it says: "Continue with the 5th Engineering tasks. Increase security, vigilance, measures in the region of Konjevic Polje. And I take it reading this doesn't refresh your recollection, any more than any of the other paragraphs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It doesn't help me, because I have to say once again: Pobudje and Konjevic Polje, in our terminology, is one thing. We don't know where the boundaries -- sometimes they refer only to Pobudje. Other times they say "Pobuje Hill." Maybe it's a problem for you when you try to determine where things are. But I have to mention there were two minefields placed there, because otherwise we hadn't -- we would not have been able to defend ourselves with the number of personnel we had. If you go from the intersection in Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac, taking the right, where the transmission lines are, that road -- that path went from the road -- that minefield went from the road to the guard post number 6. And the left side of the road, 800 to 1.000 metres from the road and parallel to the road to Bratunac, was a stretch that ended with guard post number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just reference you briefly to the final section, "Requests," paragraph 9. It says: "Assign 50 litres of oil for the above task." And we have the B/C/S on our screen. You have the original in front of you. And we can see on the VRS or B/C/S version that we have, in paragraph 6, the number "50" is circled and "50 litara nafte" is underlined, and that's in blue ink on the original. And then as we go down to paragraph 9, we have another reference to 50 litres; and then we have written in handwritten blue ink and underlined is the word "done." Now, you've got the original in front of you. Can you explain to us, in your view, who would have been the person that did this underlining and wrote in the word "done"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I can't even guess who that might be. Probably someone from the corps or -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, bringing -- if you can look at the original, just one more question. Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: As I said earlier, it probably is. My signature is not complicated. It's very easy to write.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness answered, Your Honour, but he already answered the same thing at the beginning of this examination. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are 100 per cent right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Going over the document, I looked at it and thought about it. I think it is a fair question, given --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you could have rephrased it. Anyway, let's proceed to a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to ask the Court permission to read back a bit of what this witness said on a similar subject in his interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the purpose behind this request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: To try to give the Court the best possible view of what the truth may be, and I can go into it in further details, of course, but it's probably not a good idea in the context of having the witness before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was going to direct the question. Are you trying to impeach the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In some respects, yes. And if you would like a foundation for that, that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But if we are going to discuss that, we will discuss it in the absence of the witness, in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Simanic, do you understand English, or a little bit of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Still, I think I better take some precautions. If you could escort the witness out of the courtroom for a short while, please. Does anyone of the Defence team want to contribute -- just one moment before you speak. I just want to know if there's anyone who wishes to make their position on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ostojic. I just want to have an indication so that we'd know how long this gentleman will need to stay outside. Yes, Ms. Nikolic first.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I'll be very brief. If my learned friend wants to treat this witness as hostile, I believe there is a clear procedure that was taken by this Tribunal in two cases, Brdjanin and Limaj, on the grounds that the witness is not telling the truth or that he is refusing to answer; and in that case, the Prosecutor asks leave of the Court in order to do what my learned friend announced he wanted to do in the case of Witness Simanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Let's hear from Mr. Ostojic, and then I'll give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just reserve it, to hear what my learned friend has said as a foundation, so I'm not sure I would have any response, except for until I hear actually what the foundation is, as he states on page 41, on line 18 through 21, I think. So I would reserve that to hear what my learned friend has to say first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason I have taken this step - over the last year, there's many times we could have possibly taken this step and we decided not to - was that, well, partly this was not a witness we had originally planned to call, but because of the document, because of the interest, we agreed to take part in this. But in his previous statements, he said to me very clearly that he signed this document and that he had signed blank documents, and that he did not know what this material was. What I was reading back to him was two times where he acknowledged that this was his signature. So, yes, when he says "probably," I don't think he's being completely truthful on that point. I think this witness is being you untruthful on several points. I think he is being truthful on others, and I think the Trial Chamber has got the good, tough job of figuring it out. In fact, I think it's important that we called him so that you see this, and I think it speaks light years about what this document means. So I think, in the end, it's worth it. But I do want to remind everyone this was not a Prosecution witness, but I do think it is helpful and I do think you can sort it out. And I think these last two questions -- or I can just read them to you now and we don't need to bother with the guy, frankly. I don't really care, but I want the trier of fact to be able to hear him clearly or see him clearly saying to me that, "This was my signature."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Ladies and gentlemen, I have still not been convinced by Judge Kwon and Judge Prost that such a way of proceeding should be allowed, but we've discussed it and I find myself in a minority. So you've got the go-ahead. In other words, the decision is to proceed by majority, by a majority vote, me dissenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Then I would be just reading back to him a few of the lines that we were talking about and getting his comments, and leaving it at that. Now, if Defence has an objection, I may change my mind, you know, if there's some issues there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's bring the witness back in. You know what our position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could give the witness the B/C/S version of the transcript. It's page 22, around lines 120 to 124, and I've highlighted some of them for the witness. And I'll just read back the relevant sections and ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also give us the precise interview you're talking about, because to my knowledge there was more than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the ERN number, please, and date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 12 January 2006 interview, and it's ERN T000-3088. And I'm going to page 22, and it starts on the English on line 23, where I basically refer him to the document. And he says, as he has testified: "God forbid." And then I ask him: "Can I ask you just briefly what you meant when you said 'God forbid,' what you read, can you read this?" Answer: "About 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilian and soldiers were arrested killed. And then I say: "Okay. Go ahead, take your time." And then he says: "And furthermore, even worse, I signed it."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall that part of our interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment before you answer the question. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like the Prosecutor to read until paragraph 23, the version in English, line 35-36, because that also relates to the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any problem with that? Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Do you have any problem with that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do, frankly. She can read that back, if she wishes. He does say, "Yes, most probably," and he talks about it again. But I don't think I need to go through it every time he talks about the signature. I just want to give you a flavour of what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead for the time being, and then you can raise it on cross-examination if you wish. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have that next page in front of you, and I think it's a good idea that you take a look at it to prepare yourself for any other questions. When you're asked if it's your signature, you say: "Yes, it is, most probably." Then I'd like you to go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a problem following the text in B/C/S. My learned friend said that it's page 22, lines around 120 to 124, which is impossible, but that's not the problem. On page 22, in B/C/S, that text is simply not there. It could be the last sentence is on page 24 in B/C/S, which means that the witness is probably not able to follow what the Prosecutor is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The witness has it in front of him; and if I said "120", I'm sorry. I'm reading it wrong, it's 20 through 24, and he has it before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would really like the witness to read for himself what is written on page 22, lines 22 and 23. That's precisely what the Prosecutor read in English, because it seems to me that the version we have in English is not at all the same as what we have in B/C/S. So, if the witness could read those two lines, that would be his reaction to that signature which is or isn't his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem is I find - I speak for myself - I find it difficult to follow, because I neither have the B/C/S text nor the English text. There seems to be some minor confusion as regards to the exact part of the text that he's supposed to be looking at. There is now an allegation or suggestion that the English translation does not correspond to the B/C/S text, so I think we need some assistance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to this. This is purely obstruction. It's designed to confuse the issue, where there is none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we can't say, yes, we agree or disagree with you, Mr. McCloskey, because we don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the Defence can get up and talk like that all day long, and there's nothing I can do to respond, because he's got it in front of him. He's got the outlined section in front of him. Translations are never perfect. This is a very simple thing. They -- that's what cross-examination is for. When they object like this and make these comments in cross-examination, it's unnecessary. Now, sometimes it's helpful because of translation issues, and we need to deal with them as we go. And they've done that many times and that's appreciated. This time, I can't really figure out what they're saying, so I can't really answer you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our position is as follows: Witness, you have heard the various submissions both from the Prosecution and some Defence teams. Our position is: Go ahead and answer the question that has been put to you by Mr. McCloskey, and then the rest will be dealt with on cross-examination. And I also think it's the case of you repeating your question, because a couple of minutes have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I can encapsulate both the question and Ms. Fauveau's concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the part I read, it clearly says that, "Worse yet, it's my signature," and then a page later you say, yes, it's your signature, but "probably." Can you tell us today, as you sit here, did you sign this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question first, Madame Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I answered several times to this question, that I sometimes signed blank papers, that this is most probably my signature, but I'm not certain, and that's all I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm really sorry, but the problem is that the question, such as it was asked, is not correct. It's not appropriate because the witness didn't clearly say that it was his signature in B/C/S. That's why I believe it's important for the witness to read lines 22 and 23, and particularly the end of line 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I strongly object at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, Madame Fauveau and you, Mr. McCloskey. We've already made our position clear on that. You can deal with that on cross-examination. But for the time being, let the witness answer the questions that are put to him. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if you can go to page 25 on that, on yours. That's the B/C/S. Maybe a bit on page 25 and 26. I won't read out my question. And the English is page 26, beginning with lines 2. I am specifically not setting out my question, but we'll have no objection if someone else does. But the answer is: "See, I have to explain to you now where the unit was during these days; and as far as I know - and I can only talk about things that I know - this is it. I really don't know where this guy who wrote it found this information in the first paragraph. There is what are mentioned. "This is in accordance with what I mentioned before, that I was signing blank pieces of pages which were later used to compile reports, to present in a report things about units that were not part of the Engineering Battalion. It sounds weird, stupid to me." It does indeed, sir, sound a little weird. Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I stated that I was a reserve officer, that I didn't know much about military terminology. And I still believe it was madness to introduce another unit into your own report, but these reports were done according to a stereotyped format. And it was referred to as a company of military police, but we didn't know what it was doing, what its strength was, where it was, or anything else about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you suggesting a professional officer in the Command of the 5th Engineering would not have written what was written in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
