utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I was wondering whether this 5th Engineering Battalion belonged to Drina Corps directly. Could you clarify, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go back to our structure area? I failed to ask you. Can you tell us, the unit, the 5th Engineering Battalion, what unit was it part of?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: To the corps that was our superior unit, the one above on Vlada, as far as I understand these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this document we're talking about, it's addressed to the Drina Corps Command, so the Drina Corps was your direct Command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll soon be having a break in ten minutes' time; but before that, let me get a revised estimate of cross-examinations. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Half an hour, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Ten, 15 minutes, Your Honour, if that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also 10 to 15 minutes, unless other colleagues exhaust my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were reckoning with ten minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe we will have no questions, Your Honour, but I reserve the right to use five minutes, unless on the colleagues asks the questions I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Probably ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Pandurevic, nothing. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who wishes to go first, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would ask the Chamber if you can have the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would it be okay to release the next witness? I know times change, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this, Mr. McCloskey: I have here, instead of the previously-estimated one hour 55 minutes, we now have one hour and 20 minutes, which means we won't finish with this witness today, unless we make an effort to do so. But if we make an effort to do so, I don't anticipate there would be much more time for the next one. So that's how I look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's been waiting most of the day, so it sounds like we should be able to let him go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Agreed. Twenty-five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can start again. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I had forgotten to ask one question I meant to ask. I mentioned that to the Defence counsel. It's not so directly related to all this material, so it should take very -- very brief. And it's not meant for impeachment, but it's meant for information for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Any problem for the Defence? No. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, as I think we'd said, I need to ask you: Did you have a -- get a criminal conviction in 2003 in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't need to hear about the facts of it, but can you just describe very briefly what -- what the crime was, what you were convicted of?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It was about a confirmation that I -- was based on a contract. The contract got stolen and nobody was found responsible but me. I was actually blamed for the missing contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So was this irregularity associated with a construction contract, basically?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Zivanovic. We have had an opportunity to meet, because I've already spoken to you. Sir, I would kindly ask you to look at the document that you have just been shown by my learned friend from the Prosecution, which is P2672. Can you see it clearly on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let us clarify one thing. I understood that you were not the one who drafted this document. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that you did not provide the person who did draft the document with any information?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You're referring to any information?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the first part, which is relevant to the arrest and killing of anything between 1.000 and 1.500 enemy soldiers and civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, we've started on the wrong foot. You're going too fast, both of you. You need to allow a short pause between question and answer, because otherwise the interpreters will not be able to catch up and we will get half transcripts. So please cooperate. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as you read the second sentence in the first paragraph, we have read this sentence on many occasions up 'til now: "Between 1.000 and 1.500 enemy civilian and soldiers have been arrested killed." Do you agree with me that once you read this sentence, this sentence is not clear and it could be interpreted in two ways? I'm going to give you these two options, and then I will ask you whether you agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that one of the options would be the following: First, 1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested and then killed; whereas, the second option would be this: In confronting the enemy group, the total number of killed and arrested was anything between 1.000 and 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers. In other words, a certain number were killed in conflict with the enemy; whereas, a certain number was arrested. I am talking only about the linguistic meaning of this sentence and not about its actual content, not about what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: This can be interpreted in several ways. I don't know how to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that these two options are possible?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I believe that they are possible, because there are no full stops, or commas, or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that it would be much clearer if there was a word "a" or "or" between the words "arrested" and "killed"?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I would not wish to answer that, because I am not able to interpret or understand this. This sentence lends itself to several interpretations, and it really depends on who's reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of one part of your interview that you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 15th of April, 2005. This is 1D376. I'm going to read to you just one sentence of one question or explanation provided to you by the Prosecutor when he was interviewing you. My question will be whether you remember this. This is page 25, lines from 11 through 14 in the English version, and page 24, lines from 28 through 30 in the B/C/S version. In the B/C/S version, it says: "Unfortunately, two men from your" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In relation to 1D376, I'm reminded there's no English attached to the document, so we need to attend to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's some kind of technical problem, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not everyone speaks your and the witness's language, and there are some of us who need to be able to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read the sentence. It is just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This sentence reads: "Unfortunately, two men from your unit were wounded, and the military operation in order to stop the Muslims from going through your area was absolutely legitimate, which was clearly established." This is what the Prosecutor told you on the occasion he interviewed you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: What page is that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is page 24. Would you please look at your screen? It is on your screen. Page 24.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Line 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 24 -- no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] I have another one. 1D376. 1D376, 15 April 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to complicate matters any further, but there was one on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is on page 25, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for that interruption, but we needed to verify something. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. I found it under page 25. There are two versions of this transcript. [Interpretation] It is on page 25, lines 14 through 17. Page 25. Well, again, it is not that. It seems there are three versions of the same transcript. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is I'm still feeling somewhat confused, Mr. Zivanovic, because, you know, the information that we get is scanty, but it's supposed to be to the point. If you look at page 56, line 10, your question seems to be directing the witness to his interview dated 15th of April, 2005. Now, I have an interview which dates back to the 21st of October, 2005; another interview which dates back to the 12th of January, 2006; and then a handwritten note submitted during OTP interview, which goes back to the first of these two interviews, that is, 21st of October, 2005. On the other hand, on the document itself, it says "15/4/2005." So rather than you explaining, I think it should be Mr. McCloskey. It's the same, "Mile Simanic" and "Milo Simanic" That's in the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was a mistake in the B/C/S version. I apologise. That's what's confused the issue, and the dates of the interviews are 21/10/2005, very short, almost nothing said there; and then "12/1/2006" is the -- that's the January one that we've been dealing with thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this 15th April that we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Ignore April in 2005. That's just a typo. That's the 2006 interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That was 2006. All right. I'm glad I raised it, because at least that clears what was troubling me in my mind. You know, I mean, I thought we had -- yes. But Mr. Zivanovic, you now know, more or less, what date you're talking about and which statement you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. I would just like the witness to see it on his monitor, but not if it is not possible to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, I would kindly ask you, even if you can't see this statement because of some technical problems, can you remember the sentence that I just quoted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just to help my learned friend, Mr. Zivanovic, I think the witness has the complete interview there in front of him. So all Mr. Zivanovic needs to do is point the witness to the correct page, and he will obviously find it. So there's no difficulty there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be page 25, line 14; actually, lines 14 through 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Twenty-five.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the sentence starting with the words: "Unfortunately, two men from your unit were wounded ..."?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to take more than the 30 minutes. We've barely started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give you my copy to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you put it on the ELMO. The usher doesn't hear me. Yes, she has.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this now, line 14? It says: "Unfortunately, two men from your unit were wounded. The military operation to prevent Muslims from passing through your area was absolutely legitimate, which was clearly established." Do you remember that this was said to you during your interview?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I believe so. Most probably it was, since it was recorded here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: For that reason, I would like to ask you to answer this: Did you understand from that that the possible killing of the enemy soldiers and those who arrived in the territory during the combat was legitimate? Did you understand that from the Prosecutor's words?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: You're referring to this particular sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm referring to this particular sentence.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It turns out that way, now that I look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm asking you this to clarify something that the Prosecutor asked you when he faced you with the second sentence of the previous report, in which you stated that the sentence pointed out the existence of a crime. Did you imply that the crime consisted in arresting people first and killing them after that, or did you also believe that it would be a crime to have killed these people in combat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment before you answer the question. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the form of the question. It's leading. This is not classic cross-examination. This is not a Prosecution witness in that technical sense. We can go on and on and on like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Defence agreed to have this witness called. I think a fair and concise question, a few leading ones, is fine. But if we go on like this forever in this context, I don't think it's appropriate to the context that this witness has been called. I don't think the Rules should be held as discreetly as they have in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear the wise words of Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't lead this witness through his examination-in-chief. I have to cross-examine him, and leading questions are permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are not going to change any rules and practice as yet, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Simanic, could you kindly answer the question, please. And, let me see, shall I read it out to him again? Do you remember the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that I have already answered some of it, but maybe it would be advisable if the question was read out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In answering the Prosecutor's question, when he faced you with the sentence about 1.000 to 1.500 men being killed, you said that it was a crime. Did you mean that the crime would have consisted in killing the detainees or even those who were killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I meant that it would be a crime if people were first arrested and then killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would move on to something else. Could you please look at the document 1D379. Do you agree that this is a document entitled "Overview of the Current Strength in the Units of the Drina Corps" for the months of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: That is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that in column 1 of this report, under number 1, certain units are enumerated?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get the list from the Defence that you're referring to of documents? We don't have anything. We don't need them before we begin our questions, but I believe the agreement is that we get them prior to questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It was handed. It was handed. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was sent, Mr. McCloskey. "It wasn't sent," says the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart doesn't have it, but that's okay. We'll deal with it after, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It happens with e-mails sometimes. It takes longer to get there, and sometimes it gets lost. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see, therefore, in column 1 of this report, that various units of the Drina Corps are enumerated; and can you find, in line 4, the 5th Engineering Battalion? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that, in column 2, we see that -- we see the name of the commander of this battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in July 1995, in the 5th Engineering Battalion, there were two active duty officers and seven reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Probably. I really don't know the numbers, but I know that we had two active duty officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says here there was one active duty NCO and 13 reserve NCOs?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I know about the one active duty NCO. I think 13 is the correct number for the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were 111 soldiers and all of them were reservists?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see, do you agree that, in the last column, we see the total strength of the 5th Engineering Battalion in July 1995, and that it was 134 men?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Most probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague from the Prosecution showed you the second part of that document 2672, which states what various units of your battalion were engaged in on that day. Do you agree there were four companies and one platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes, only on paper, not in terms of actual strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the strength stated in this document, it is clear that not every company could have 100 or more men, but now I'm trying to find out something different. Could you explain this: We see that there were four companies and one platoon. One platoon is smaller than a company?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Was it three companies or four?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw four companies in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's document P2672, if we can show it again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Here, look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So we see the first two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see that four companies are enumerated here: Pioneer, Road and Bridge Company, Engineer Company, and Pontoon Company. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there were four of them?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree those soldiers we saw on the list, 111 engineers and their superior officers, were assigned to those four companies and one platoon?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was the number even across the four companies?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No. It was not evenly distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Some companies were stronger, others not?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The Engineering Company had the highest -- the largest number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you give us a rough estimate, how many men there were in the Pioneer Company?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I believe around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please look at this item A.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I conclude, from subparagraph (a), that the Pioneers Company was assigned to four different tasks. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One part of it was in Pobudje, another on Vis feature, yet another in the area of Derventa, and the fourth one had been to Zeleni Jadar and had just returned that day?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that each of these groups had approximately the same number of men? In other words, if there was a total of 20, each group had 5 or so?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Explain, then.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The largest group was at Vis feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing first. When you are sending soldiers to remove mines, you send two or three soldiers; and then if these mines are explosives and then have to be removed and transported, you send assistants from appropriate companies because they are the only ones who are trained for that job. If they are laying a minefield, then you send, again, two, possibly three, and the unit to which they are sent gives them assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You say that the group at Vis feature was the largest one?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How many men, approximately, were there?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Around ten. There should have been around ten, but I'm not sure, because they were not the only ones who were engaged there. There were men from other companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From this answer you've just given, explaining how many men are normally sent to remove mines and how many there were at Vis feature, I conclude that, in the area of Pobudje, there were five or six men, if the whole company had 20. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Well, look, if we take it that those who had come back from Zeleni Jadar, then there couldn't have been more than five.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Reading your interview, I noticed that, on several occasions, you mentioned that those people who belonged to your battalion were not really young men, closer to middle age.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: A lot of them were actually retired, but their retirement procedure was not complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement - and I'm not going to repeat this - it says that on the 13th of July, two soldiers from your unit were wounded. Would you please just look at P2879.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] The second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the details of the two men who were wounded. You probably remember their names. This document may serve as a reminder. Please look at the column which is entitled "Data and Place of Birth." Is it correct that the first man was born in 1943?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: They must have copied it from some sort of record. It should be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That would have made him 53 at the time he was wounded in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The second man, Vaso Orasanin, was born in 1939, and he was 56 when he was wounded; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, I did not manage to find any more details about the personnel of the 5th Engineering Battalion, so I would appreciate your answer. Were the others approximately in the same age group as these two men?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Except the Pioneers, everyone was approximately in that age group; old hands, worn out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to 2672, please, and look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you look at paragraph 6, where we can read that 50 litres of oil is required for the burial of enemy soldiers who were killed. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I don't know how much fuel a construction machine like that would need to dig a pit to bury a number of people, could you tell me how large a pit can a construction machine of the kind that you had at the time dig? What could be the size of that pit?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Can we say a pit, a hole?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It all depends on the distance that has to be covered to go there and back. The machine that we had uses 15 litres per hour, so that's approximately two, two and a half hours of work, assuming that there is a stretch of road to be covered as well on the way there and back. And the pit would be one metre deep, three by two, unless it's rocky terrain. It had to be normal ground, because our machine was rather weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "three by two, one metre deep," does it mean the length and breadth would be three and two metres respectively, and depth would be one metre?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that in a pit like that, it would be impossible to bury the number of people that is mentioned in paragraph 1 of that report that we have read?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have spoken to the Prosecution more than once. As far as I could see from your interviews, you emphasised that you did not write this report yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we scroll down a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the end, we see two initials, "MB/MB." Generally speaking, what do these initials represent?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: They should be the initials of the man who typed and the man who wrote, who drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That means that the person in this case both drafted and typed the document, judging by the initials?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Right, judging by the initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: In your talks with the Office of the Prosecutor, were you ever informed if that person had been contacted, if that person had any comments to make concerning this report, or yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, just to -- my name is John Ostojic. I represent Mr. Beara here today in this case. I have several questions for you. I was hoping we would conclude, but it honestly doesn't look like we can, unless I speak very quickly, which I will not do. If we can stick with that same document on the second page that we had, P02672, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I hate to interrupt you, but we've only got five minutes. So try to limit the topic to fit those five minutes, and we'll continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm taking it somewhat out of my outline to go to this topic. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, again we're looking at the -- and I think you had the original there, but in any event we're looking on the e-court screen, where it has, on the left-hand corner there, the initials "MB/MB." Do you know who "MB" was in 1995 in the 5th Engineering Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Mirko, whom we called Zajo; and, later on, I learned that his family name was Bastric, or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How did you learn that information; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: When I spoke to the Prosecutor, I could not remember at the time. It was only later on that I remembered, because we all used his nickname. That's why I couldn't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so I'm clear, so it was the Prosecutor who told you who this individual was with the initials "MB"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who did, then?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I stated that before the Prosecutor, when he asked me about that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And was this something during the interview on July 12th, 2006 -- January, January. I'm sorry. January 12th, 2006. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I believe you'll find it somewhere in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll take a look at that a little closer, and we'll get back to it tomorrow. Just before the break, I want to ask you a couple of questions, because you were asked by the Prosecutor about crimes, et cetera. Did you ever discuss with him what a legitimate combat task was on January 12th, 2006?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: Whose task are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to your battalion's combat task. Did you discuss with the Prosecutor, in January of 2006, relating to your combat task and whether or not it was legitimate?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. It was only mentioned in his question, as I have just been able to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember discussing with the Prosecutor -- and it's just for two minutes and we'll address it more tomorrow. Do you remember that the Prosecutor told me -- told you that he didn't have any indication that the 5th Engineering Battalion murdered anybody at the Kravica warehouse? Do you remember him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that he said that there were no indications about the 5th Engineering Battalion having killed anybody in Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And also do you remember telling him that he didn't think the 5th Engineers killed these people? Do you remember that on a separate occasion when he was questioning you in January of 2006?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor interviewed me only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that, and we'll address it. I think it might be a good time to stop, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, Mr. Ostojic. So, Witness, Mr. Simanic, look at me, please. Mr. Simanic, we are stopping here for today, and we will continue and finish tomorrow, in the morning. Between now and tomorrow, when you resume your testimony and conclude it, you're not to talk to anyone or let anyone talk to you or try to discuss or mention to you the subject matter of your testimony. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, 4th September, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
